I'm 65 years old, and I've been farming my six mu of land in Quzhou since I was a young man. I only finished primary school, but I know my fields better than any book. It's early March now, and my wheat is starting to green up after the winter. I walk the field every morning — the plants look decent this year, not too much winter kill.

I've got six mu total, and I'll stick with what I know: winter wheat on all six mu, then summer maize on the same land right after the wheat comes off in early June. I thought about cotton, but I'm getting older and my back hurts when I bend down too much. Picking cotton is too much labor for me now, and my sons work in the city and can't help much. Wheat and maize give me two harvests and I can sell both easily to the grain buyers who come to the village.

For the wheat, I planted an improved variety last October — the same one my neighbor Lao Zhang uses, it does well here. I did rotary tillage before planting, broke up the soil nicely. Now I need to irrigate soon, probably in the next week if it doesn't rain. I'll water three times this spring: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The pump electricity costs money, but if I skip irrigation the yield drops too much. I'll put down about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu — I use compound fertilizer as base and topdress with urea when the wheat is jointing. I also put some phosphate and potash, maybe 5 kg P and 3 kg K per mu. The fertilizer prices went up again, but my nephew told me last year he cut back too much and regretted it, so I'd rather use a bit more than too little. I'll spray twice for pests — herbicide once and insecticide once when I see aphids.

For the summer maize, I'll plant right after harvesting the wheat. There's no time to plough — everyone in my village uses no-tillage for the maize, just broadcast or drill the seed into the wheat stubble. I'll use hybrid seed, Nongda or something similar from the seed shop. The maize needs less work than wheat. I'll irrigate twice if it's dry, and spray maybe three times — herbicide once at planting, and insecticide a couple times because the corn borer always shows up. I don't put as much fertilizer on the maize as the wheat, maybe 14 kg N, 4 kg P, and 2 kg K per mu. The soil is still warm from the wheat and the stubble gives some nutrients back.

I expect about 450 kg per mu from the wheat if the weather holds, and maybe 500 kg per mu from the maize. That's enough to feed my wife and me, sell the rest, and have some cash for my grandson's school fees. I won't get rich, but I won't go hungry either.
